title: A merit function approach for direct search
contribution: Extends directional direct search to nonlinear, possibly nonsmooth, derivative-free constraints. Relaxable constraints are handled by an l1 merit-function acceptance test plus a Restoration mode, and unrelaxable ones by an extreme barrier. The paper proves Clarke-stationarity results for every Restoration regime.
problem_entry: Classifies constraints by evaluation status (relaxable vs unrelaxable, including hidden constraints). It then positions itself as a merit-function alternative to the filter-based progressive barrier of Audet–Dennis, the only prior general approach handling both types (pp. 1–3).
key_idea: Keep the search/poll/step skeleton and redefine only success. A step succeeds on sufficient decrease of the violation g when far from feasibility, otherwise on sufficient decrease of M = f + mu_k g. mu_k is a derivative-free transcription of the classical penalty update. Restoration is entered when g falls while f rises a lot (pp. 3–6).
assumptions: f and c_i locally Lipschitz near limit points; f bounded below; nonempty hypertangent cone of Omega_nr; refining directions dense in the relevant cones. The infinite enter/leave-Restoration case additionally needs no step increase, no search step and convergent iterates, which the authors call 'not the ideal ones'. No bound on the penalty parameter is assumed (pp. 2, 7–12, 17).
proof_devices: case split by Restoration recurrence: finitely often / entered and never left / entered and left infinitely often (p. 4)
three-branch contradiction for lim inf alpha_k = 0, where a merit-success with the ratio-defined mu_k is impossible by construction (p. 7)
Clarke–Jahn derivative along refining directions with Lipschitz swap of d_k for d and rho(alpha)/alpha -> 0 (pp. 8–11)
density of refining directions in T^Cl(x*) or T(x*) gives Clarke stationarity (pp. 9–11)
mean value theorem with limit PSS D* for the smooth particularization (pp. 13–14)
experiments: Proof of concept: untuned MATLAB, no search step, random unit directions |D_k| in {n/2, n+1, 2n}, 40 seeds. Three problems from the progressive-barrier paper (two with n = 50, plus the styrene truth model via NOMAD's C++ code), each from feasible and infeasible starts. Plots of f vs evaluations; compared with progressive barrier only through its published numbers. Restoration was entered a negligible number of times (pp. 14–16).
positioning: 'An alternative approach to progressive barrier [6]'; credits MADS and Vicente–Custódio as the two ways to globalize with an extreme barrier; lists augmented-Lagrangian, penalty, restoration and filter methods neutrally; notes that model-based TR has no constrained convergence theory (pp. 2–3).
writing: One-sentence novelty claim in the abstract; reusable boxed 'Begin … End' definitions; roadmap by case; §7 translates Clarke results into smooth gradient language; hedged numerics ('proof of concept', 'relatively promising'); a referee simplification is reported and declined (pp. 1, 4–5, 13–14, 17).
limits_future: States: extra conditions in the infinite-switch case; no comprehensive comparison; random directions/PSS study under way; effect of search step, mu-bar and step resetting open (pp. 12, 17). Unstated: no complexity, three test problems, Restoration theory barely exercised, no code release (pp. 14–16).

title: Globally convergent evolution strategies
contribution: Makes the (mu/mu_W, lambda)-ES class, including CMA-ES, globally convergent to Clarke-stationary points. The change is minimal: a separate step size contracted on failed sufficient decrease and reset to the ES step on success. Three decrease variants are proved and benchmarked.
problem_entry: The ES community has no global convergence results for recombining ES (only asymptotic (1, lambda) results). The paper sets out to bridge DFO and ES, which are separated by terminology, and defines global convergence as display (1) (p. 2).
key_idea: Change Algorithm 2.1 'in a minimal way'. Keep ES sampling, selection, recombination and the CMA updates. Add sigma_k separate from sigma^ES, impose sufficient decrease (mean/mean, max/max or max/mean), contract sigma_k on failure and set sigma_{k+1} = max{sigma_k, sigma^ES_k} on success (pp. 4–6, 11).
assumptions: f bounded below and Lipschitz near x*; normalized recombined directions a_k (or each d^i_k) dense in the sphere along the refining subsequence, with ||a_k|| bounded away from zero; a weight condition (2) for the max versions. Density is argued with probability one for Gaussian directions (pp. 6–10).
proof_devices: lim inf sigma_k = 0 by contradiction per version, using weight condition (2) to transfer max-decrease to the mean (pp. 6–7)
Clarke analysis along the recombined direction a_k with Lipschitz correction r_k <= nu ||a_k/||a_k|| - d|| (p. 8)
backtrack to the last successful iteration, where frozen x^mu and condition (2) give a standard no-decrease inequality at x_k (pp. 9–10)
probabilistic density: every spherical cap has probability >= eta for Gaussian a_k, plus resampling when ||a_k|| < eps (p. 9)
experiments: CMA-ES with Hansen's default parameters, rho = 1e-4 sigma^2. Moré–Wild 53 problems x 4 classes; data profiles (50n budget; 1e-3, 1e-7) and performance profiles (f* from 500000-evaluation runs; 1e-2, 1e-4). Version ablation (mean/mean best). Against pure CMA-ES and NOMAD/MADS without models, losses are reported. Global check on 19 BBOB multimodal functions with 20 starts and medians, where pure CMA-ES is slightly better (pp. 10–18).
positioning: Bridges ES (Rechenberg, Beyer–Schwefel, Hansen; asymptotic analyses by Auger, Jägersküpper, Greenwood–Zhu) and DFO. Explains why the MADS lattice does not fit continuous ES sampling and follows the sufficient-decrease line (Vicente–Custódio, Coope–Price, KLT). Constructive toward ES (pp. 2–3, 8).
writing: Single framing question; original and modified algorithms printed side by side; Newton-without-line-search analogy; assumptions discussed after the theorem; proof difficulty admitted; measured numerical claims; the naming slip 'mean/max' appears twice (pp. 3–6, 9, 15–17; proof difficulty p. 5; slip pp. 5, 11).
limits_future: States: only CMA-ES tested; interaction with the CMA updates not understood; CMA's implicit derivative information unused; search step with quadratic models and the constrained case left to a forthcoming paper (pp. 18–19). Unstated: no complexity; weight condition (2) not enforced in the runs; no code release (p. 11).

title: On the optimal order of worst case complexity of direct search
contribution: Proves |D|/cm(D)^2 >= c n^2 for every positive spanning set. Hence the n^2 factor in the known O(n^2 eps^-2) and O(n^2 eps^-1) direct-search evaluation bounds cannot be improved by choosing another PSS; D-plus is optimal up to a constant.
problem_entry: Asks whether the n^2 in existing WCC bounds is an artefact of D-plus. Rewrites the bounds as O(m kappa^-2 eps^-a), which turns the question into min over PSS of |D|/cm(D)^2 (problem (6)) (pp. 1–2, 5).
key_idea: Cosine measure equals a sphere-covering radius: a unit PSS with cm = kappa covers the sphere with caps of radius arccos kappa, and cm(D) is the largest such kappa. A discrete-geometry covering bound then caps cm(D) <= zeta sqrt(n^-1 log(|D|/n)) (pp. 6–8).
assumptions: f C^1 with Lipschitz gradient and bounded below; rho = C alpha^p with p = 2 fixed; PSS with cm >= kappa, |D| <= m and bounded norms; search step costing at most a multiple of m. 'Optimal' refers to the n-order of the upper-bound expression over PSS choices, not to an oracle lower bound (pp. 3–5, 8).
proof_devices: equivalence lemma: cosine measure <-> spherical covering by caps of radius arccos(cm) (pp. 6–7)
imported covering bound from discrete geometry (Tikhomirov 2015 and earlier results) (p. 7)
log x <= x - 1 to finish (p. 8)
rewrite the WCC bound as m kappa^-p-hat to expose the design trade-off (pp. 4–5)
experiments: none (Fig. 1 plots |D|/cm(D)^2 for uniform 2-D PSSs, p. 6)
positioning: Completes the authors' WCC line ([20], [9]); credits Konečný–Richtárik's simpler rederivation, noting its restriction; imports discrete geometry with explicit thanks to that community; closes by comparing with GRVZ probabilistic descent O(mn eps^-2) (pp. 2, 7–9).
writing: Nine pages; abstract states the result and the proof idea; guiding question posed in the text; κ explained as the price of missing gradient information, by analogy with randomized coordinate descent; open problems listed precisely with status (n = 3, 4 known; n >= 5 open) (pp. 1, 4, 8).
limits_future: Problems (6) and (12) open; optimality of D-plus for m = 2n open for n >= 5 (p. 8). The result concerns bounds for deterministic PSS polling; the implied direction is randomization (p. 8).

title: Worst case complexity of direct search under convexity
contribution: Proves that sufficient-decrease directional direct search on smooth convex functions needs O(eps^-1) iterations and O(n^2 eps^-1) evaluations to reach ||grad f|| < eps, with a 1/k rate in f and global r-linear rates for f and x under strong convexity. This is the first deterministic DFO method with the convex gradient-method order.
problem_entry: Uses the gradient-method yardstick: the bound improves to O(eps^-1) under convexity, and Nesterov's random Gaussian DFO attains it only in expectation. Can a deterministic zero-order method match it? Direct search is chosen as the simplest setting (p. 2).
key_idea: No algorithmic change (except an optional step cap M for p != 2). Port Nesterov's convex proof to direct search: at unsuccessful iterations ||grad f|| = O(alpha); charge successes to the nearest unsuccessful iteration; telescope 1/Delta f; count unsuccessful iterations by a log of step ratios (pp. 3–15).
assumptions: f convex, C^1 with Lipschitz gradient; nonempty solution set with R = sup over the level set of dist(., X*) finite (holds without bounded level sets, e.g. f = y^2; fails for sqrt(x^2 + y^2) - x); PSS with cm >= cm_min; step cap M if p != 2; strong convexity results with p = 2 only (pp. 6–8, 16, 23).
proof_devices: at unsuccessful iterations ||grad f|| <= omega_g^-1 alpha^min(1,p-1) (Cor. 3.1, p. 7)
convexity + R: Delta f_i <= R ||grad f(x_{k_i})|| (p. 9)
reciprocal telescoping of 1/Delta f over unsuccessful-iteration indices (p. 9)
log counting |U| <= omega1 |S| + omega2 + log_beta2(...) (pp. 10–11)
ln x <= x to absorb the log term (p. 12)
midpoint split of successful iterations for the gradient bound, mirroring the k..2k argument (pp. 13–14)
strong convexity: ||grad f||^2 >= 2 mu (f - f*) gives a (1 - 2 omega mu) contraction per success (p. 17)
experiments: Tables of average evaluations over 20 runs. Nesterov's quadratic for n = 2–16: direct search (D-plus, gamma = 1, rho = 1e-3 t^2) far beats one-point Gaussian and beats two-point Gaussian even though the latter gets exact r0 and nu ('a huge advantage'). Five convex CUTEr problems at n = 8: direct search better 'overall', though two-point Gaussian wins on arglinc at every accuracy (not mentioned in the text). No profiles (pp. 19–23).
positioning: Places itself in the WCC literature (Nesterov, CGT sharpness and FD-ARC, Garmanjani–Vicente smoothing). Novelty counted precisely: second DFO method with O(eps^-1), 'but the first time for a deterministic approach'. Improves Dolan–Lewis–Torczon's local r-linear result on three stated points (pp. 2, 19, 22).
writing: Abstract of three results stated relative to the gradient method; §2 recaps the gradient proofs that §4 mirrors; notation paragraph on O-constants; parameter commentary (gamma = 1 optimal); pathological example in the conclusion; advantage given to competitors disclosed (pp. 1, 3–6, 22–23).
limits_future: States: Assumption 4.1 can fail; p != 2 needs the cap M; strong convexity for p = 2 only (pp. 7, 16, 23). No future-work section; constants complicated and not optimized; no code release (pp. 11, 15, 18, 22–23).

title: Full-low evaluation methods for derivative-free optimization
contribution: A DFO framework that alternates expensive Full-Eval line-search iterations (FD-BFGS in practice) with cheap Low-Eval direct-search iterations (probabilistic [d, -d] polling). A switch couples the two step sizes. Theory gives a gradient-descent-type rate when Full-Eval keeps succeeding and Clarke stationarity when it fails; the method is robust across smooth, nonsmooth and noisy problems.
problem_entry: Diagnoses that each DFO paradigm (direct search, FD line search, model-based TR, untheorized hybrids) fits only some regimes. Aims at one rigorous class with 'sustainedly good performance across all possible function types' (pp. 2–4).
key_idea: A Full-Eval step counts only if its line-search step beta >= gamma rho(alpha_k), where alpha_k is the direct-search step; otherwise switch to Low-Eval. Successful Full-Eval steps then act as direct-search search steps. Switch back after as many consecutive Low-Eval failures as the last Full-Eval's backtracks (pp. 5–6, 10, 14).
assumptions: Smooth: C^1 with L-Lipschitz gradient; ||grad f - g_k|| <= u_g beta_k ||g_k|| (ensured by a criticality-step FD loop); angle and size conditions on p_k. Nonsmooth: 'Full-Eval Failure' (||g_k|| bounded away from 0 on successful Full-Eval), bounded iterates, Lipschitz f near x*, dense refining directions. Noise not covered by theory; the implementation fixes h = sqrt(eps) (pp. 2, 7, 10–13).
proof_devices: lower bound on the backtracked step from Taylor plus failure of beta_k/tau (Lemma 3.1, pp. 7–8)
decrease >= M ||g_k||^2 per successful Full-Eval, giving min ||grad f|| = O(1/sqrt(ns_k)) (p. 8)
PL inequality for a linear rate under strong convexity (pp. 9–10)
coupling (2.2) turns Full-Eval successes into forcing-function decreases, so alpha_k -> 0 by summability (Lemma 3.2, pp. 10–11)
standard refining-direction Clarke argument (pp. 11–12)
criticality-step loop for FD gradients with finite termination by contradiction (pp. 12–13)
experiments: Six solvers (Full-Low, BFGS-FD, pDS, DFO-TR, FDLM, NOMAD). 62 smooth CUTEst problems (n = 2–51), 12 scalable problems at n = 40 and 80, and 53 Moré–Wild problems (piecewise smooth; additive and multiplicative, deterministic and stochastic noise at 1e-3). Performance profiles (2000n budget) and data profiles (100(n+1) budget). Losses reported per class (DFO-TR on small smooth problems and additive deterministic noise; NOMAD on stochastic noise). Number of runs for randomized solvers not stated (pp. 13–22).
positioning: Surveys paradigms with balanced pros and cons; places Vicente's own SID-PSM/MFN hybrids among those without comprehensive theory; claims 'To our knowledge such type of rigorous results is novel in DFO'; contrasts with FDLM's explicit noise estimation; separates its terminology from the surrogate framework of Booker et al. (pp. 2–4, 15).
writing: Abstract pairs 'For the theory, we consider' with 'In practice,'; the key design move is flagged twice; results explained per class; overall-best claim without a combined profile; minor slips (tau for theta and I_SL twice in Lemma 3.2's proof; 'four other approaches' followed by five) (pp. 1, 5, 11, 13–14, 20–22).
limits_future: Future: bound and linear constraints, larger dimensions, other Full/Low instantiations (TR with fully linear models, simplex gradients, deterministic DS; Gaussian smoothing) (p. 24). Unstated: rate counts only successful Full-Eval iterations with no total-evaluation complexity; no noise theory; h and criticality step differ between theory and code; switching rule not analysed; no code release (pp. 2, 6, 8, 12–14).
